Distinct from authorization: authentication comes first, then permissions apply

slides.title: Authentication: The Gatekeeping Function
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Lifecycle Management, is the primary federal standard governing authentication design.

Exam tip: If a scenario distinguishes 'who are you' from 'what can you do,' the first is authentication, the second is authorization.
content_blocks: Authentication is the gatekeeping function every other endpoint control depends on. A device can be flawlessly patched and hardened, yet remain totally compromised the instant an attacker obtains valid credentials to log into it, no exploit required, no vulnerability chained, just a working username and password.

This topic examines how credentials are stored, how they are attacked, and how modern authentication design mitigates both. The throughline connects directly to Topic 4.1's endpoint vulnerabilities: hardening a device's software is meaningless if the front door (the login prompt) can simply be walked through.

slides.title: Why Plaintext Passwords Are Never Stored
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: A cryptographic hash function is one-way, deterministic, and exhibits the avalanche effect.

Misconception: Students often think 'encrypted' and 'hashed' passwords are the same, encryption is reversible with a key, hashing is (ideally) one-way and irreversible.
bullets: Well-designed systems never store a user's actual password
Instead they store the output of a cryptographic hash function applied to it
Login: hash the entered password, compare to the stored hash
A stolen database yields hashes, not usable passwords, without further cracking

slides.title: Why Plaintext Passwords Are Never Stored
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: A cryptographic hash function is one-way, deterministic, and exhibits the avalanche effect.

Misconception: Students often think 'encrypted' and 'hashed' passwords are the same, encryption is reversible with a key, hashing is (ideally) one-way and irreversible.
content_blocks: A well-designed system never stores a user's actual password. Instead, it stores the output of a cryptographic hash function applied to that password. When a user logs in, the system hashes the newly entered password and compares the result to the stored hash, if they match, authentication succeeds, and the plaintext password itself is never retained on disk.

This design means that even if an attacker steals the entire credential database, they do not automatically obtain usable passwords; they obtain hashes, which they must then attempt to reverse or guess through separate cracking techniques.

slides.title: Fast Hashes vs. Password Hashing Algorithms
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Modern GPUs compute roughly 10 billion unsalted MD5 hashes/second but only a few thousand bcrypt hashes/second, a five-to-six order of magnitude gap.

Exam tip: 'Fast' is good for checksums, 'bad' for passwords, this framing resolves most exam distractors about hash choice.
bullets: General-purpose hashes (MD5, unsalted SHA-256) were designed for SPEED
Speed is a feature for file integrity checks, a liability for password storage
Password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2) are deliberately SLOW
Slowness dramatically reduces attacker guesses-per-second even on GPU/ASIC rigs

slides.title: Fast Hashes vs. Password Hashing Algorithms
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Modern GPUs compute roughly 10 billion unsalted MD5 hashes/second but only a few thousand bcrypt hashes/second, a five-to-six order of magnitude gap.

Exam tip: 'Fast' is good for checksums, 'bad' for passwords, this framing resolves most exam distractors about hash choice.
content_blocks: Not all hash functions are appropriate for password storage, one of the most frequently misunderstood concepts in introductory security education. General-purpose hash functions such as MD5 and unsalted SHA-256 were designed for speed: verifying file integrity, indexing data structures. That same speed becomes a liability when applied to passwords, since it lets attackers test enormous numbers of guesses per second.

Password hashing algorithms, bcrypt, PBKDF2, and Argon2, are purpose-built to be intentionally slow and resource-intensive, dramatically reducing the guesses-per-second an attacker can attempt even with specialized cracking hardware.

slides.title: Salting: Defeating Precomputation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-63B section 5.1.1.2 mandates a salt of at least 32 bits, generated using an approved random bit generator.

Misconception: The salt is not a secret key, its job is uniqueness, not confidentiality.
bullets: A salt is a random string unique per password, combined before hashing
Stored alongside the hash, does NOT need to be secret, only unique
Without salting, identical passwords produce identical hashes
Salting forces attackers to attack each hash individually, not the whole DB at once

slides.title: Salting: Defeating Precomputation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-63B section 5.1.1.2 mandates a salt of at least 32 bits, generated using an approved random bit generator.

Misconception: The salt is not a secret key, its job is uniqueness, not confidentiality.
content_blocks: Password hashing alone is insufficient without salting. Without a salt, two users who choose the same password produce identical hashes, and an attacker can precompute hash values for common passwords once and reuse that precomputed table against any stolen database (a rainbow table attack).

Salting defeats this by ensuring that even identical passwords hash to entirely different values, forcing an attacker to attack each hash individually rather than reusing precomputed work across the whole database.

slides.title: Anatomy of a bcrypt Hash String
slides.speaker_notes: Critical Concept: A common misconception is that the salt must be kept secret like a password. It does not, its purpose is uniqueness, not secrecy. What must stay secret is the plaintext password, which is never stored at all.
content_blocks: To make 'slow hashing' concrete, consider how bcrypt and PBKDF2 encode their computational cost directly into the stored hash string. The bcrypt hash $2b$12$R9h/cIPz0gi.URNNX3kh2OPST9/PgBkqquzi.Ss7KIUgO2t0jWMUW breaks down as: $2b$ algorithm identifier, 12 cost factor (2^12 = 4,096 rounds), a 22-character base64 salt, and a 31-character hash output.

The salt is embedded directly within the stored string, it does not need to be kept secret, only unique per password. On login, the system extracts the algorithm identifier, cost factor, and salt from the stored string, re-hashes the submitted password using those exact same parameters, and compares the result.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: bcrypt has a lesser-known limitation: a maximum input length of 72 bytes.

Exam tip: Argon2id is the current OWASP-recommended default because it adds memory-hardness on top of a configurable work factor.
content_blocks: bcrypt, based on the Blowfish cipher, incorporates a configurable cost factor controlling exactly how expensive each hash computation is. PBKDF2 achieves the same effect by repeating an underlying hash function (commonly SHA-256) a configurable number of iterations, NIST SP 800-132 recommends a minimum of 10,000 iterations, though modern guidance pushes this much higher given hardware improvements.
Because both work factors are adjustable, administrators can raise the cost for newly hashed passwords as attacker hardware improves, without changing the underlying algorithm.

slides.title: Multi-Factor Authentication: Independent Factor Categories

quiz.question: A system requires a password plus the answer to a security question. Does this qualify as multi-factor authentication?
choices: Yes, two credentials were required
No, both are knowledge factors from the same category
Yes, because it takes longer to bypass
No, because security questions are biometric
quiz.explanation: MFA requires proof from independent factor categories (know/have/are). A password and a security question are both knowledge factors, so this is not true MFA.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-63B section 4.3 defines Authenticator Assurance Levels (AAL1-AAL3); AAL2 and above require MFA.

Misconception: Two passwords, or a password plus a security question, is NOT MFA, both are knowledge factors. True MFA needs independent categories.
bullets: Knowledge factor: passwords, PINs, vulnerable to all four attack types
Possession factor: hardware tokens, TOTP apps, SMS codes
Inherence factor: biometrics, cannot be guessed/stuffed but cannot be reset
MFA requires proof from at least TWO independent categories

content_blocks: Modern authentication design mitigates password attacks by requiring more than a password alone. Multi-Factor Authentication combines factors from independent categories so a single compromised element (e.g., a stuffed password) is insufficient on its own: knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have), and inherence (something you are).

TOTP codes are generated by combining a shared secret key with the current time via HMAC, changing every 30 seconds so a stolen code becomes useless almost immediately. Biometric authentication cannot be guessed or stuffed, but raises distinct concerns since a biometric trait cannot be reset the way a password can.

slides.title: Case Study: RockYou Breach (2009)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RockYou is the canonical teaching example for why plaintext storage is a total, irrecoverable failure, no after-the-fact hardening can protect credentials already exposed in readable form.

Exam tip: If a scenario says passwords were 'stored as entered' or 'readable in the database,' that is plaintext storage, the worst-case failure mode.
content_blocks: In December 2009, RockYou suffered a breach exposing approximately 32 million accounts. The critical failure was RockYou's storage practice: passwords were stored in plaintext, with no hashing whatsoever. When the database leaked, attackers obtained every user's actual password directly, with no cracking required at all.

The leaked list, rockyou.txt, revealed staggering patterns in human password choice (the most common password was simply '123456') and became one of the most widely used dictionary-attack wordlists in the industry.

content_blocks: In June 2012, LinkedIn disclosed a breach ultimately exposing roughly 167 million credentials. LinkedIn had hashed passwords using SHA-1, a fast, general-purpose hash never intended for password storage, and critically, without any salt.

Because the hashes were unsalted, attackers applied precomputed rainbow tables and massively parallelized GPU cracking to recover most plaintext passwords within days. The exposed dataset was compiled into wordlists used in credential-stuffing campaigns against other services for years afterward.

Many usernames + one source IP + rapid timing = credential stuffing

slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: Always look for the lockout event itself in the log, it confirms a specific numeric threshold (e.g., 5 attempts) and tells you the control that ultimately stopped the attack.
content_blocks: Given a raw authentication log excerpt, the exam expects you to classify the attack type from observable patterns alone: how many distinct usernames are targeted, whether the source IP is singular or distributed, and how tightly clustered the timestamps are. A single username targeted by many password attempts in sequence suggests brute-force or dictionary; many different usernames tried rapidly from one source IP suggests credential stuffing, since the attacker already possesses a list of real username/password pairs and is simply testing which still work.

bullets: Model how a work-factor slows guess throughput
Even a small cost-factor increase multiplies total cracking time
Legitimate single login stays fast; brute-force at scale becomes impractical
This is the same mathematical principle behind bcrypt's cost factor

slides.title: Practice: Simulating a Slow Hash's Cost
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This simulation is a simplified illustration, not real bcrypt, the point is the multiplicative relationship between work factor and total attacker time, not the exact numbers.
content_blocks: The snippet below models, in simplified Python, how increasing a password hashing algorithm's work factor multiplies the time required to test a large number of password guesses, while adding negligible delay to a single legitimate login. Run it to see the guesses-per-second drop as the simulated cost factor rises.

slides.title: Practice: Simulating a Slow Hash's Cost
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This simulation is a simplified illustration, not real bcrypt, the point is the multiplicative relationship between work factor and total attacker time, not the exact numbers.

code_block.content:
import time

def simulated_hash(password, cost_factor):
    """Simulate a slow password hash: 2^cost_factor trivial rounds."""
    rounds = 2 ** cost_factor
    x = hash(password)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        x = hash((x, password))
    return x

for cost in (8, 12, 16):
    start = time.time()
    simulated_hash("Tr0ub4dor&3", cost)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"cost_factor={cost:>2}  rounds={2**cost:>7}  elapsed={elapsed:.4f}s")

# Notice elapsed time roughly doubles each time cost_factor increases by 1 --
# the same design principle bcrypt uses to stay ahead of faster attacker hardware.

slides.title: Application: Choosing Controls for a Given Scenario
slides.speaker_notes: Misconception: 'Just make employees change passwords more often' is never the best answer once a specific technical control gap has been identified in a scenario.
bullets: Plaintext storage found -> migrate to salted Argon2id/bcrypt immediately
Unsalted fast hash found -> add per-password salt + move to slow algorithm
Credential-stuffing pattern detected -> deploy MFA, not just password resets
Quarterly forced rotation policy -> replace with breach-list screening + MFA

slides.title: Application: Choosing Controls for a Given Scenario
slides.speaker_notes: Misconception: 'Just make employees change passwords more often' is never the best answer once a specific technical control gap has been identified in a scenario.
content_blocks: Given an exam scenario, match the observed weakness to the specific hardening control that addresses it, rather than a generic 'improve security' answer. Plaintext storage requires migrating to a salted, purpose-built slow hash. An unsalted fast hash requires adding a unique salt and switching algorithms. A credential-stuffing pattern is only fully addressed by MFA, since the attacker already has valid-looking credentials from elsewhere. An outdated forced-rotation policy should be replaced per current NIST guidance, not merely reinforced.

slides.title: Synthesis: The Credential Attack Kill Chain
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: On an FRQ, walk this chain explicitly and name which control breaks which link, salting breaks link 2, lockout breaks link 3, MFA breaks link 4.
bullets: 1. Reconnaissance: attacker sources leaked credentials or plaintext dumps
2. Weak storage exploited: unsalted/fast hash cracked, or plaintext read directly
3. Credential testing: brute-force, dictionary, rainbow table, or stuffing applied
4. Authentication bypass: valid-looking credentials submitted at the login endpoint
5. MFA is the last line: an independent factor category can still block entry

slides.title: Synthesis: The Credential Attack Kill Chain
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: On an FRQ, walk this chain explicitly and name which control breaks which link, salting breaks link 2, lockout breaks link 3, MFA breaks link 4.
content_blocks: Chaining this topic together: an attacker's path to unauthorized access typically begins with a storage failure (plaintext, or hashed without salt/slow algorithm) somewhere, either at the target or at an unrelated service whose leaked data gets reused. That failure produces crackable or directly usable credentials, which are then tested against a target's login endpoint using brute-force, dictionary, rainbow table, or credential-stuffing techniques depending on the data available. Account lockout and rate limiting can slow this stage. If the attacker still submits a valid password, MFA remains the final, independent barrier, the only control in this chain that does not depend on the password itself being strong.
